topics.title: Build an Emergency Fund
topics.hook: One surprise bill can wreck your finances. Here's how to stop that from happening.
points: An emergency fund is cash set aside only for true emergencies, like a job loss or a car repair.
Most experts suggest saving three to six months of essential expenses.
Start small. Your first goal is just one thousand dollars.
Keep it in a high yield savings account so it earns interest but stays easy to reach.
extras: Automate a small transfer every payday so you never have to think about it.
If you have to use it, pause other goals and refill it first.

topics.title: The 50/30/20 Budget Rule
topics.hook: If budgeting feels impossible, try the simplest rule in personal finance.
points: Split your take home pay into three buckets.
Fifty percent goes to needs, like rent, groceries, insurance and minimum debt payments.
Thirty percent goes to wants, like eating out, hobbies and streaming.
Twenty percent goes to your future: savings, investing and paying off debt faster.
extras: If your needs are above fifty percent, that's your signal to cut housing or transport costs.
It's a starting point, not a law. Adjust the numbers to fit your life.

topics.title: Pay Yourself First
topics.hook: Wealthy people don't save what's left after spending. They do the opposite.
points: Paying yourself first means you save before you spend anything else.
The moment your paycheck lands, a set amount moves straight into savings or investments.
You then live on whatever is left, so saving never depends on willpower.
Even ten percent, automated, adds up to serious money over the years.
extras: Raise the percentage by one point every time you get a raise and you'll barely notice it.

topics.title: How Your Credit Score Works
topics.wiki: Credit score in the United States
topics.hook: Your credit score can cost you thousands. Here's what actually moves it.
points: Payment history is the biggest factor, so never miss a due date.
Next is utilization: try to use less than thirty percent of your credit limit.
The age of your accounts matters too, so think twice before closing your oldest card.
Lots of new applications in a short time can drag your score down.
extras: Set every card to autopay at least the minimum and you'll protect the biggest factor automatically.

topics.title: The Real Cost of Credit Card Debt
topics.hook: Paying only the minimum on your credit card is a trap. Here's why.
points: Credit cards often charge twenty percent interest or more per year.
Interest is charged on your unpaid balance, so a small debt can grow fast.
Paying only the minimum can stretch a few thousand dollars of debt over many years.
Pay the full statement balance every month and you pay zero interest.
extras: Carrying a balance? Attack the highest interest card first. That's called the avalanche method.

topics.title: Debt Snowball vs Debt Avalanche
topics.hook: There are two famous ways to crush debt. Which one is right for you?
points: With both methods, you pay the minimum on every debt and throw extra money at one target.
The avalanche targets the highest interest rate first. It saves the most money.
The snowball targets the smallest balance first. Quick wins keep you motivated.
The best method is the one you'll actually stick with.
extras: When one debt is gone, roll its payment into the next one. That's where the momentum comes from.

topics.title: High Yield Savings Accounts
topics.hook: If your savings sit in a regular bank account, you're probably leaving money on the table.
points: Traditional big banks often pay almost nothing on savings.
High yield savings accounts, usually from online banks, can pay many times more.
In the United States they're typically FDIC insured, just like regular accounts.
They're perfect for your emergency fund and short term goals.
extras: Rates change over time, so compare a few banks before you switch.

topics.title: Lifestyle Inflation
topics.hook: Why do people who earn more often feel just as broke? It's called lifestyle inflation.
points: Lifestyle inflation is when your spending rises every time your income does.
A nicer car, a bigger apartment, more takeout. Each upgrade feels small.
Together they quietly eat every raise you ever get.
The fix: save at least half of every raise before you get used to it.
extras: Upgrade on purpose, not on autopilot. Pick the one thing that truly makes you happier.

topics.title: Sinking Funds
topics.hook: Christmas, car insurance, vacations. They're not surprises, so stop treating them like ones.
points: A sinking fund is money you save a little at a time for a known future expense.
Take the total cost and divide it by the months until you need it.
Save that amount every month in a separate account or bucket.
When the bill arrives, the cash is already waiting.
extras: Many online banks let you create multiple named savings buckets for free.

topics.title: Calculate Your Net Worth
topics.hook: There's one number that tells you how you're really doing with money.
points: Your net worth is everything you own minus everything you owe.
Add up cash, investments, retirement accounts and the value of your home or car.
Then subtract loans, credit card balances and any other debt.
Track it every few months. The trend matters more than the number.
extras: A negative net worth is normal early on, especially with student loans. Just keep it moving up.

topics.title: The Power of Compound Interest
topics.hook: Albert Einstein supposedly called it the eighth wonder of the world. It's compound interest.
points: Compound interest means you earn returns on your money and on your past returns.
At a ten percent yearly return, money roughly doubles every seven years.
That means time in the market matters more than almost anything else.
Starting at twenty five instead of thirty five can leave you with roughly twice as much.
extras: Use the rule of seventy two: divide seventy two by your return to estimate the years to double.

topics.title: Why Index Funds Win
topics.hook: Most professional fund managers fail to beat a simple, boring investment.
points: An index fund buys every stock in an index, like the S&P 500.
Instead of picking winners, you own the whole market.
Fees are tiny, and over long periods most actively managed funds trail the index.
Warren Buffett has said most people are best off in a low cost index fund.
extras: Look at the expense ratio. A fraction of a percent can mean tens of thousands saved over decades.

topics.title: Dollar Cost Averaging
topics.hook: Scared to invest because the market might crash tomorrow? Use this strategy.
points: Dollar cost averaging means investing the same amount on a regular schedule.
When prices are high, your money buys fewer shares. When prices drop, it buys more.
You stop trying to time the market, which almost nobody does well.
It turns investing into a habit instead of a guessing game.
extras: Most brokers let you automate recurring investments in a couple of minutes.

topics.title: Stocks vs Bonds
topics.hook: Stocks and bonds are the two building blocks of almost every portfolio. Here's the difference.
points: When you buy a stock, you own a small piece of a company.
When you buy a bond, you're lending money in exchange for interest payments.
Stocks usually grow more over time, but they swing up and down a lot more.
Bonds are steadier, which is why many investors add more of them as they near retirement.
extras: The mix of stocks and bonds you hold is called your asset allocation, and it drives most of your results.

topics.title: Don't Put All Your Eggs in One Basket
topics.hook: The only free lunch in investing, according to a Nobel prize winner, is diversification.
points: Diversification means spreading your money across many different investments.
If one company or sector crashes, the rest of your portfolio can cushion the blow.
You can diversify across companies, industries, countries and asset types.
A single broad index fund can give you hundreds of companies in one purchase.
extras: Owning ten tech stocks isn't diversification. They tend to move together.

topics.title: Roth vs Traditional Retirement Accounts
topics.hook: Roth or traditional? This one choice decides when you pay taxes on your retirement money.
points: With a traditional account, you get a tax break now and pay taxes when you withdraw.
With a Roth account, you pay taxes now, and qualified withdrawals in retirement are tax free.
If you expect a higher tax rate later, Roth usually wins.
If you're in a high bracket today, traditional can make more sense.
extras: Can't decide? Many people split contributions between both for tax flexibility.

topics.title: Never Skip the 401(k) Match
topics.hook: There's free money sitting on the table at most jobs, and millions of people ignore it.
points: Many employers match part of what you put into your 401k.
A common match is fifty cents for every dollar, up to six percent of your salary.
That's an instant fifty percent return before your money is even invested.
At minimum, contribute enough to get the full match.
extras: Check your vesting schedule. Some matches only become fully yours after a few years.

topics.title: Hidden Fees Eating Your Returns
topics.hook: A one percent fee sounds tiny. Over a lifetime, it can cost you a fortune.
points: Funds charge a yearly fee called an expense ratio.
That fee comes out every year, whether the fund makes money or not.
Over thirty or forty years, a one percent fee can eat a large share of your final balance.
Low cost index funds often charge a small fraction of that.
extras: Always check the expense ratio before you buy any fund.

topics.title: What To Do When the Market Crashes
topics.hook: The stock market will crash again. What you do next decides how rich you get.
points: Historically, the US stock market has recovered from every major crash.
The biggest mistake investors make is selling in a panic and locking in losses.
Some of the best days in the market come right after the worst ones.
If you're investing for the long term, a crash can mean stocks are on sale.
extras: Keep an emergency fund so you never have to sell investments at the bottom.

topics.title: How Dividends Work
topics.hook: Imagine getting paid just for owning a stock. That's what dividends are.
points: A dividend is a share of company profits paid out to shareholders.
Many mature companies pay them every quarter.
You can take the cash, or reinvest it to buy more shares automatically.
Reinvesting dividends has been a huge part of the stock market's long term return.
extras: A sky high dividend yield can be a warning sign, not a bargain. Always check why.

topics.title: What Is an ETF?
topics.hook: ETFs are one of the easiest ways to start investing. Here's how they work.
points: ETF stands for exchange traded fund.
It's a basket of investments, like stocks or bonds, that trades on an exchange like a single stock.
One share can give you exposure to hundreds or thousands of companies.
Many ETFs have very low fees, which makes them popular for long term investors.
extras: Unlike traditional mutual funds, you can buy or sell ETFs any time the market is open.

topics.title: What Is Bitcoin, Really?
topics.hook: Everyone talks about Bitcoin, but few people can explain it in thirty seconds. Let's fix that.
points: Bitcoin is digital money that isn't controlled by any bank or government.
Transactions are recorded on a public ledger called the blockchain.
Only twenty one million bitcoin will ever exist, which is why some call it digital gold.
Its price is famously volatile, so never invest more than you can afford to lose.
extras: Bitcoin was launched in two thousand nine by an anonymous creator called Satoshi Nakamoto.

topics.title: Hot vs Cold Crypto Wallets
topics.hook: Not your keys, not your coins. Here's what that crypto saying really means.
points: A crypto wallet stores the private keys that prove you own your coins.
A hot wallet is connected to the internet. Convenient, but more exposed to hackers.
A cold wallet keeps your keys offline, often on a small hardware device.
If you leave coins on an exchange, you're trusting that exchange to hold them for you.
extras: Never share your seed phrase with anyone. Anyone who has it can take everything.

topics.title: Crypto Scams to Avoid
topics.hook: Billions are lost to crypto scams. These are the red flags to watch for.
points: Anyone promising guaranteed returns is lying. Real investments carry risk.
Be careful with giveaways that ask you to send crypto first. That money is gone.
Watch for fake support accounts that message you asking for your seed phrase.
Romance and investment scams often build trust for weeks before asking for money.
extras: If it sounds too good to be true, it is. Especially in crypto.

topics.title: What Are Stablecoins?
topics.hook: Most crypto swings wildly in price. Stablecoins are designed not to.
points: A stablecoin is a cryptocurrency pegged to a stable asset, usually the US dollar.
Many are backed by reserves of cash and short term government bonds.
Traders use them to move money quickly without leaving the crypto world.
But stable doesn't mean risk free. Some have lost their peg in the past.
extras: Always check who issues a stablecoin and what actually backs it.

topics.title: Inflation Explained
topics.hook: Why does everything cost more every year? Here's inflation in thirty seconds.
points: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over time.
When prices rise, each dollar you hold buys a little less.
Many central banks aim for about two percent inflation per year.
Cash sitting idle loses value, which is why investing matters.
extras: At three percent inflation, prices roughly double in about twenty four years.

topics.title: How Interest Rates Affect You
topics.hook: When the Federal Reserve changes interest rates, your wallet feels it. Here's how.
points: The Fed sets a target for the rate banks charge each other overnight.
When it raises rates, mortgages, car loans and credit cards get more expensive.
But savings accounts usually start paying more interest.
When it cuts rates, borrowing gets cheaper and savings yields tend to fall.
extras: The Fed raises rates to cool inflation, and cuts them to support a slowing economy.

topics.title: What Is a Recession?
topics.hook: Everyone fears the R word. But what actually is a recession?
points: A recession is a significant, widespread decline in economic activity.
A common shorthand is two straight quarters of shrinking GDP.
During recessions, unemployment usually rises and businesses cut back.
Recessions are a normal part of the economic cycle, and every one has ended.
extras: The best preparation: an emergency fund, manageable debt, and staying invested for the long run.

topics.title: GDP in Plain English
topics.hook: GDP is the number that shows up in every economic headline. Here's what it means.
points: GDP stands for gross domestic product.
It's the total value of all goods and services a country produces.
In the United States, consumer spending makes up the largest share of it.
When GDP grows, the economy is expanding. When it shrinks, it's contracting.
extras: GDP per person is often a better way to compare living standards between countries.

topics.title: Side Hustle Taxes
topics.hook: Making money on the side? Don't let taxes catch you off guard.
points: In the US, side hustle income is generally taxable, even if you don't get a tax form.
On top of income tax, self employed people usually owe self employment tax.
A simple habit: set aside about a quarter to a third of what you earn.
Track business expenses. Many of them can reduce what you owe.
extras: If you owe enough, you may need to make estimated tax payments during the year.

topics.title: Turn a Skill Into Income
topics.hook: You probably already have a skill someone would pay for. Here's how to find it.
points: Write down what friends and coworkers already ask you for help with.
Writing, design, editing, tutoring and spreadsheets are all in steady demand.
Start with one small paid project to prove people will pay.
Then raise your price as your reviews and confidence grow.
extras: Reinvest your first earnings into tools or training that let you charge more.

topics.title: Multiple Streams of Income
topics.hook: Relying on one paycheck is risky. Here's how people build multiple income streams.
points: Your job is your first stream. Protect it and grow it first.
Next, add active income, like freelancing or a side business.
Then build passive streams, like dividends, interest or digital products.
Each new stream makes losing any single one less scary.
extras: Passive income usually takes a lot of upfront work or money. Be wary of anyone saying otherwise.

topics.title: Rent vs Buy
topics.hook: Is renting really throwing money away? It's not that simple.
points: Buying builds equity, but comes with extra costs like taxes, insurance and repairs.
Mortgage interest, especially early on, is money you never get back either.
Renting offers flexibility and frees up cash that you can invest.
A common rule: buying makes more sense if you'll stay at least five years.
extras: Budget roughly one to two percent of a home's value per year for maintenance.

topics.title: 15 vs 30 Year Mortgage
topics.hook: Your mortgage term can change how much your home really costs by a huge amount.
points: A thirty year mortgage has lower monthly payments, so it's easier on your budget.
A fifteen year mortgage has higher payments but usually a lower interest rate.
Over the life of the loan, the fifteen year can save you a huge amount of interest.
Pick the payment you can comfortably afford, even in a bad month.
extras: Extra principal payments on a thirty year loan can shorten it without locking you in.

topics.title: Invest in Real Estate Without Buying a House
topics.hook: You don't need to be a landlord to invest in real estate.
points: A REIT is a company that owns income producing real estate.
Think apartments, warehouses, offices, cell towers and data centers.
US REITs generally must pay out most of their taxable income as dividends.
You can buy them like a stock, sometimes for the price of a single share.
extras: REIT dividends are often taxed as ordinary income, so they can fit well inside retirement accounts.
